How this board works

  • Notes (left) stay put while you pan and zoom and save themselves as you type. Drag the bottom-right corner to resize; click the title to fold. Everything is also written into content/_board_thumbs/board_notes.txt — connect it once with Connect board_notes.txt; after a Chrome restart one click on the notes reconnects it.
  • One lane per video, oldest first. Every card = one shot: its start frame, its clip, and under Prompts the exact image prompt, clip prompt, attachments, other takes and notes.
  • Two approvals per video. Frames first: FRAME FOR REVIEW → FRAME APPROVED. Then clips, animated only from approved frames: CLIP FOR REVIEW → APPROVED (or REJECTED → re-rolled as the next take). Take numbers always match the file name.
  • Approve / Reject appear only on cards waiting for you. Each click copies one line for Claude; Review (bottom right) shows only the waiting cards; Copy decisions copies all your lines at once — paste them to Claude.
  • Source of truth: prompts, settings and attachments come from the Higgsfield job that made each file, matched on 2026-09-23 — clips byte-identical to their Higgsfield result (md5), frames by exact file size. A card says so where a file could not be matched. Full history of every take: content/video_N_assets/prompts.md § Verified record.

Playbook — what holds a shot together

  1. Chain by job_id, not by adjective. To hold a face, a house or a wall across two shots, pass the earlier generation’s job as an extra reference and write “REFERENCE IMAGE N is the shot to reproduce” or “governs the wall, house, ground and background — reproduce them exactly.” Describing the same house again in prose drifts every single time.
  2. Assign every reference a job in the first two lines. They arrive as REFERENCE IMAGE 1, 2, 3 in submission order. Say what each one controls and what it must not contribute — “composition and crop only, ignore its room, its colours, its text overlay.” An unassigned reference leaks its content into the render.
  3. The unlit strand close-up is always REFERENCE IMAGE 1 on any shot with the curtain in it. It is the only thing that makes the product read as string lights rather than a screen. The anti-panel block in content/curtain_realism/ goes in verbatim alongside it — pasted, not paraphrased, not trimmed.
  4. Different surface? Override the block, do not edit it. One line ahead of it: “SURFACE OVERRIDE: wherever the block says ‘garage door’, read ‘gable end siding wall’ — everything else applies exactly as written.” Rewriting the block itself is how it quietly stops working.
  5. Empty space has to be described as an object. Clear sky for a text overlay, a bare sofa cushion, a wall with no windows — all of it renders only when written out positively and then fenced with a ban list: “nothing resting on it: no boxes, no bags, no blankets.” “An empty sofa” produces a full one.
  6. “Switched off” renders as “absent”. An unlit curtain has to be described as hardware — dull cold-grey plastic beads, dark wires, sag, uneven hem — and given a light source to catch: a street lamp raking across it. Otherwise the model returns a bare wall.
  7. Describe the grip, not the object. For anything held, say what each hand is doing and where the rest of the mass goes. “A dozen strands bundled and compressed together between her fingers” plus “pools on the snowy ground beside the step stool” reads; “holding the curtain” gives an empty hand.
  8. No text on the artwork, ever — and the ban has to be loud. Left alone the model turns every gag into a caption spelled across the house. The line that holds: “NO TEXT, NO LETTERS, NO WORDS, NO NUMBERS, NO SIGNS anywhere in the light artwork or anywhere in the photo.”
  9. Comedy as a situation, not a punchline. Santa with a beer, Santa raiding the fridge, a reindeer visibly fed up with waiting — these read from the street in chunky bulbs. Anything that needs reading, or that tips past cheeky into crude, does not survive as an ad.
  10. Wall colour is a lighting decision. White bulbs vanish on near-black brick. Pale greige, cream or light siding is what makes the product visible at all — pick the surface before the scene.
  11. Change one thing at a time. Feed the approved frame back, restate what must not move, then label the edit “CHANGE ONE THING ONLY”. Never rewrite a prompt that already worked.
  12. Every prompt carries the look clause. “Hyper realistic, crisp real-estate-photography clarity, evenly exposed, sharp focus front to back… NOT cinematic, no colour grading, no vignette, no shallow depth of field, no bloom, no CGI polish.” Drop it and the frame turns into a movie still.

v21_c02_g1.pngjob a790f95b — Side-on eye-level camera with the sofa behind and to the right of her. The v20 C2 animation would not transfer onto it.
Notes from the round
File name

The old board listed v21_c02_g2.mp4 as the clip in the cut and marked it lost. This take is on disk as v21_c02_g1.mp4: its Higgsfield job carries the same clip prompt and its frames match the export (checked 2026-09-23). The 2026-09-18 naming migration left it under the earlier take number.

What made it work

State the camera as a sentence of its own, at the top, and repeat it as a negative. “COPY THE CAMERA AND STAGING OF REFERENCE IMAGE 1 EXACTLY. This is the most important instruction.” followed by “Do not move the camera to the side, do not shoot her from the front, do not put the sofa behind her.” Describing the sofa’s position relative to her (“DIRECTLY IN FRONT OF HER, filling the right half and the bottom-right, running diagonally away”) is what fixed it.

Regenerate without breaking a chain. Passing take 1’s own job back in as a reference kept the woman identical, so the already-approved C3 stayed valid.

What made it work

Speed is a structure problem, not an adjective problem. Piling on “slowly”, “unhurried” and “no fast motion” does nothing while the timeline still asks for three things. The fix was to delete a whole beat and stretch the two survivors to 2.0s each, then add a paragraph that says out loud why the deleted beat is missing: “THAT IS THE WHOLE CLIP… cramming it in is exactly what would force the footage to look sped up.”

“A clearly different pose every half second” is itself a speed-up instruction. That line was in every take-1 prompt and it is what taught the model to snap between poses. It was replaced with a continuous-but-unhurried rule: always moving, never hurried, every change flowing into the next at natural human speed.

Give it permission to end mid-action. “It is far better that she is still mid-reach as the clip ends than that any part of it looks fast-forwarded” removes the model’s incentive to compress, because finishing the action is no longer the goal.

v21_c05_g1.pngjob 105df508 — Artwork read pixelated, dim and dull. The anti-panel block’s own “extremely low resolution and blocky” clause was the cause.
Notes from the round
What made it work

The anti-panel block fights the LED-wall look by making the picture coarse — and that is exactly what reads as boring. Split the two concerns: keep every physical construction rule (vertical strands, see-through to the siding, point-source bulbs, sag, uneven hem, no bezel/backing panel) but raise the strand density instead of lowering the resolution — “many thin vertical wires, DENSELY spaced, each carrying many small round bulbs closely spaced along it, so the curtain has plenty of resolution and the picture reads cleanly… faint vertical dotted structure still runs through the artwork.”

Add a positive quality directive and a reference to point at. “THE ARTWORK MUST LOOK BEAUTIFUL AND HIGH QUALITY… rich saturated colour, strong clean shapes, bright confident linework and real charm. Do NOT make it dull, dim, muddy, crude, chunky, blocky, coarse or low-resolution” — with v20 C7 attached as the standard.

Notes from the round
File name

The old board listed v21_c07_g2.mp4 as the clip in the cut and marked it lost. This take is on disk as v21_c07_g1.mp4: its Higgsfield job carries the same clip prompt and its frames match the export (checked 2026-09-23). The 2026-09-18 naming migration left it under the earlier take number.

What made it work

“Covers the wall” has to be spelled out as coverage. “THE LED CURTAIN COVERS THE ENTIRE GABLE WALL — edge to edge, corner to corner, all the way up into the peak of the gable and all the way down to the ground. No bare wall left showing around it.”

One character beats a busy scene at this distance. A single big Santa with a sack and a wreath reads instantly from across the street; the multi-element scenes turn to mush once the bulb grid coarsens.

What made it work

The lit rectangle has to be described as a cage, not as a picture. Naming every part that could escape — paw, ear, end of the string, scarf — and saying that each one is forbidden from touching an edge works far better than one blanket “stays inside”.

Tell it which way to resolve the conflict. “If a pose would take a limb out to an edge, THE POSE IS MADE SMALLER — the rectangle is never made bigger to fit it.” Without that sentence the model grows the curtain instead of shrinking the drawing.

Jaw clenched, eyebrows down and pulled together, nostrils flaring, teeth showing, muttering and swearing under his breath with his mouth working the whole time. Notes from the round
What made it work

Name the empty space as an object. “Leave room for text” does nothing. “The TOP FIFTH OF THE FRAME IS CLEAN EMPTY OVERCAST SKY with nothing in it — not the roof, not the gutter, not a branch, not a wire” survives even a big camera move.

One change per generation. g6 attaches g4 and says “CHANGE ONE THING ONLY: MOVE THE CAMERA MUCH CLOSER”, then explicitly re-locks the pose, the decorations, the house and the weather. Five takes of re-describing the scene got nowhere; one take of naming the single change landed it.

What made it work

Write the curtain as strands, never as a surface. Vertical dotted lines of light, wider gaps sideways than up-and-down, see-through to the wall behind, uneven wavy hem. The moment it is allowed to be a flat sheet it renders as an LED video wall and the shot dies.

The camera has moved about 30 degrees round to her side — a slightly more side-on three-quarter angle, a little lower, closer to the level of the sofa seat, so we now see the lid edge in profile and read the pivot clearly. Still HELD IPHONE, LOCKED FOCAL LENGTH, handheld micro-shake only, NO ZOOM. LID MECHANISM, GEOMETRICALLY. The box is a magnetic-closure flip-top. Notes from the round
What made it work

Attach the frame and name only what changes. The take that worked is about 110 words: “@Image 1 is the photo. Keep it EXACTLY as it is… CHANGE ONLY TWO THINGS: a different woman, a different room.” Four prompts of 300–450 words describing the same geometry all drifted. Long geometric description competes with the attached reference and wins.

Open the reference before writing about it. Three of those five takes were written from a description of the v20/v21 frame rather than the frame itself. The sofa is in front of her, not beside her — one look would have saved three generations.

What made it work

Speed is a structure problem, not an adjective problem. Piling on “slowly”, “unhurried” and “no fast motion” does nothing while the timeline still asks for three things. The fix was to delete a whole beat and stretch the two survivors to 2.0s each, then add a paragraph that says out loud why the deleted beat is missing: “THAT IS THE WHOLE CLIP… cramming it in is exactly what would force the footage to look sped up.”

“A clearly different pose every half second” is itself a speed-up instruction. That line was in every take-1 prompt and it is what taught the model to snap between poses. It was replaced with a continuous-but-unhurried rule: always moving, never hurried, every change flowing into the next at natural human speed.

Give it permission to end mid-action. “It is far better that she is still mid-reach as the clip ends than that any part of it looks fast-forwarded” removes the model’s incentive to compress, because finishing the action is no longer the goal.

Notes from the round
File name

The old board listed v22_c06_g2.mp4 as the clip in the cut and marked it lost. This take is on disk as v22_c06_g1.mp4: its Higgsfield job carries the same clip prompt and its frames match the export (checked 2026-09-23). The 2026-09-18 naming migration left it under the earlier take number.

What made it work

The blocky-grid block and the beautiful-artwork block cannot both be in one prompt. They pull in opposite directions and the blocky one wins. g2 drops the “low resolution, chunky stepped edges, no smooth curves” paragraph and uses the C5/C7 wording instead — “DENSELY spaced, many small round bulbs closely spaced along it, so the curtain has plenty of resolution” — while keeping every see-through rule.

What made it work

A crowd that waits and then reacts always looks staged. The rewrite bans the build-up outright: they are neighbours hanging about, chatting to each other, glancing at the lights and back at their friends, attention drifting on and off the garage the whole time.

Start the clip mid-action, explicitly at 0.0s. “AT 0.0s, IN THE VERY FIRST FRAME, EVERY PERSON IS ALREADY MID-MOVEMENT” plus named examples (already mid-laugh, already turning, already raising a cup) removes the frozen opening beat.

Stagger the beats so nothing happens in unison. Half-second rows, each naming two or three different people doing unrelated things, produce a group that reads as alive rather than choreographed.

Notes from the round
What made it work

The canonical C2 framing is v20 C2 g5, not v21 and not v22. Three takes drifted because the v22 frame was the one attached. Once v20_c02_g1.png went in as @Image 1 with “reproduce the camera, framing and sofa placement EXACTLY”, it landed first try.

Describe the geometry you can see, not the geometry you remember. Take 2 failed because the correction itself was written from memory. The sofa is ahead of her and recedes diagonally into depth; it does not run flat across the frame. Opening the reference before writing the fix would have saved a generation.

What made it work

Speed is a structure problem, not an adjective problem. Piling on “slowly”, “unhurried” and “no fast motion” does nothing while the timeline still asks for three things. The fix was to delete a whole beat and stretch the two survivors to 2.0s each, then add a paragraph that says out loud why the deleted beat is missing: “THAT IS THE WHOLE CLIP… cramming it in is exactly what would force the footage to look sped up.”

“A clearly different pose every half second” is itself a speed-up instruction. That line was in every take-1 prompt and it is what taught the model to snap between poses. It was replaced with a continuous-but-unhurried rule: always moving, never hurried, every change flowing into the next at natural human speed.

Give it permission to end mid-action. “It is far better that she is still mid-reach as the clip ends than that any part of it looks fast-forwarded” removes the model’s incentive to compress, because finishing the action is no longer the goal.

What made it work

Notes from the round
What made it work

Two references need two explicit, single jobs — stated before any description. “@Image 1 governs FRAMING, CAMERA and POSE ONLY” and “@Image 2 governs WHO THE WOMAN IS ONLY” are the first two lines of the prompt. Without that split the model blends the two rooms and you get a third room that is neither.

Stripping app UI off a screenshot reference needs the full list, not the category. “No app interface” is not enough. The prompt names them one by one — heart, comment and share icons, play button, speaker icon, caption, username, profile picture, status bar, comment bar — and closes with “no text of any kind anywhere in the picture.”

What made it work

When a take keeps going wrong, change the action, not the adjectives. Two re-rolls off the same start frame both drifted. What fixed it was Daniel replacing the motion outright — she throws the lights down on the sofa — rather than another pass of “more natural”. A prompt can steer an action it can already do; it cannot rescue an action the model keeps misreading.

Shorten the clip to fit the action. The picked take is the only 4-second generation in the lane. Five seconds left slack the model filled with invented motion; four seconds is exactly one throw.

“Held iPhone” has to be written as a negative. Because Daniel asked for a held-iPhone shot, the prompt had to state that nothing of the operator is visible — no phone, screen, hand, fingers, arm, sleeve or device anywhere in frame — or the model puts a phone in the picture.

If the action does not fit comfortably, SLOW THE ACTION DOWN; never speed the footage up. It is far better that she is still mid-reach as the clip ends than that any part of it looks fast-forwarded. CAMERA — HELD IPHONE, LOCKED FOCAL LENGTH. Portrait, exactly the framing and the angle of the reference image, looking slightly up at the wall. Handheld micro-shake only — a few pixels of organic drift. ABSOLUTELY NO ZOOM IN, NO ZOOM OUT, NO PUSH IN, NO PULL BACK, NO DOLLY, NO CRANE, NO ORBIT. The wall, the white gutter, the brick garden wall and the stool stay exactly the same size in frame from the first frame to the last, and the camera never swings round to an oblique or corner-on view of the wall. MOVEMENT RULE: she is never frozen and never hurried. Her body is in continuous unhurried motion the whole four seconds — weight shifting on the stool, shoulders rolling, ribs breathing, curls swinging and settling, the puffer jacket creasing and rustling, the strands swaying on after every touch. But every change FLOWS smoothly into the next at natural human speed. She never snaps, never jitters, never stutters between poses, and no limb ever travels faster than a real arm travels. ACTION TIMELINE (4 seconds, one continuous take, no cuts) — ONLY TWO THINGS HAPPEN, AND BOTH ARE SLOW: 0.0-2.0s — she lifts the gathered bundle in her right hand and shakes it out ONCE, slowly and heavily. The shake takes well over a full second of screen time: her arm swings out and down, the tangled net lets go in stages rather than all at once, and a long sheet of black strands falls open down the slate-blue boards and swings for a moment before it settles. The loose coil on the snow drags and shifts with it. 2.0-4.0s — still up on the stool, she stretches both arms high and presses the header wire up under the lip of the white gutter, her thumbs working slowly along it, then walks her hands a short way sideways to her RIGHT along the roofline, onto the bare stretch of wall beyond the strands she has already hung, pressing and tucking as she goes, her torso twisting and her heels lifting and dropping on the tread. She is STILL tucking when the clip ends. The curtain sways gently against the boards and is still settling on the last frame. THAT IS THE WHOLE CLIP. She does NOT step down off the stool, does NOT step back, does NOT plant her hands on her hips and does NOT tilt her head back to look at her work. There is no time for any of that at real speed, and cramming it in is exactly what would force the footage to look sped up. She stays on the stool from the first frame to the last. THE LED CURTAIN IS BLACK — CRITICAL. The wire is BLACK, not white and not clear. Every vertical strand hanging down the wall is a thin BLACK cord and the unlit bulbs on it are small and DARK. Against the slate-blue boards the strands read as thin dark lines. The heaped bundle on the snow is a tangle of BLACK cord, clearly dark against the white snow. No white wire, no clear wire, no silver wire appears at any moment. HARD RULES: the curtain is COMPLETELY OFF the entire time — not one bulb lights, no glow, no colour, no animation on the wall. The wall never gains windows, doors or new features, the white gutter and downpipe never move and the red-brick garden wall never changes. The strands are separate vertical strands obeying gravity, sagging slightly, with an uneven wavy bottom hem — never a flat sheet, never a panel, never a screen. The loose coil rests in the snow with real contact shadows. Her face is never shown; she stays turned away from camera throughout. No other people enter frame. NO TEXT, NO LETTERS, NO WORDS, NO NUMBERS, NO CAPTIONS, NO SUBTITLES, NO WATERMARK anywhere in the video. AUDIO: natural room sound only — no music, no score, no background song. Cold outdoor winter ambience, thin plastic strands rattling and clicking against wood siding, a step-stool creak, boots on a metal tread, boots compressing snow, one quiet effortful breath. No voice. LOOK: real iPhone UGC. Flat overcast winter daylight, slightly cool white balance, mild sensor noise, natural skin, no cinematic grade, no lens flare, no slow motion, no speed ramp, no fast motion. The whole clip plays at normal 1x speed from first frame to last.

Notes from the round
What made it work

Generate the still beat, not the action — the action belongs to the video. The frame is deliberately the moment BEFORE the kick: feet flat, fists clenched, jaw set. Putting the kick in the start frame gives the clip nothing left to do.

Headroom is a one-change edit, not a re-prompt. g2 reproduces g1 in an exhaustive inventory and then says “CHANGE ONE THING ONLY”. Re-describing everything is what stops the room, the tree and the man drifting while the crop moves.

A reference can be attached for a single detail. g1 used Daniel’s “Christmas Decor in 1965” screenshot for one thing — the wide duct-tape bands spiralling down the tree with figures taped flat to the branches — with its room, staircase, ladder and woman explicitly excluded.

What made it work

First take, no re-roll — because the start frame already held the pose. The clip only had to release a tension the frame had already built. Prompt skeleton as in V24: locked-handheld CAMERA block, timed TIMELINE bands, AUDIO block, realism tail, no-operator-visible negative. Shouted line verbatim: “I’M DONE WITH THIS! DONE!”

Written dry on purpose. Natural room sound only, no music and no score — Daniel adds the music in CapCut, and a scored clip fights whatever he drops on top.

Notes from the round
What made it work

“Space at the top” means a thin strip, not a band of sky. Eight passes bounced between “too little space at the top” and “too much space and the camera it’s too far away”, because the model treats headroom and camera distance as the same dial. They have to be given separately and in the same sentence: keep the subject this size, add this much empty sky.

Once the angle is right, freeze it in words. g9 opens with “THE ANGLE IS CORRECT AND MUST NOT CHANGE” and then describes it geometrically — the roof edge enters LOW at the LEFT edge and exits HIGH at the RIGHT edge. Edge-by-edge geometry survives a chained edit; “more oblique” and “like @Image 1” do not.

What made it work

Ban the tilt the fall would otherwise justify. “The man falls out of the LOWER part of the frame; the camera does NOT follow him down.” Without it the model reads a fall as permission to tilt, which throws away the framing that took eight passes to win.

Say it is comedic. “Comedic, nobody is hurt” keeps a slip-and-fall from being generated as an accident. Shouted line: “OH COME ON!”

They fall in a slight arc, they never fall straight and boring, and they land on the bottom band of the picture. LAYER THREE — ELVES RUN ALONG THE BOTTOM BAND CATCHING THEM. Small chunky ELF figures, lit in bright green and red with pointed hats and curled-toe boots, run in from just inside the left edge and just inside the right edge of the curtain along the very bottom of the picture. They scurry left and right underneath the falling presents with a big bouncy stomping stride, knees lifting high and hats bobbing, arms stretched out in front of them, and they CATCH the falling presents and stack them into a growing pile on the bottom band. When an elf catches one it bobs down with the weight, adds it to the pile, waves both arms in celebration and scurries off after the next one. The pile of presents on the bottom band GROWS visibly wider and taller across the four seconds. There are always at least two elves running in opposite directions, so the bottom of the picture is never empty and never still. LAYER FOUR — THE STAR TRAIL STREAMS. The trail of small stars behind the team continuously chases backwards away from the sleigh, one star lighting as the one ahead of it goes out, an endless streaming ripple that never stops for the whole four seconds. ELF AND PRESENT CONTAINMENT: the elves are SMALL — no taller than the sleigh is deep — and they stay in the BOTTOM BAND of the curtain the whole time, always below the reindeer's hooves. They enter from just INSIDE the left and right edges and run out to just INSIDE those same edges — they never touch an edge, never cross it, never appear on the stucco, the spruces, the lamp post or the driveway. They never climb, never jump high, never reach the sleigh. The presents fall only inside the rectangle and only in the band BETWEEN the sleigh and the bottom of the picture — no present ever falls out of the bottom of the curtain. The growing pile spreads SIDEWAYS along the bottom band, never upward toward the team, and always keeps the clear dark margin below it and at both sides. THE ANIMATION IS RELENTLESS FROM FRAME ONE. THE BIGGEST MISTAKE WOULD BE A QUIET START. At 0.0s the artwork is already mid-cycle, already loud, already changing, two presents are already mid-fall and two elves are already mid-stride — the picture does NOT switch on, does NOT hold still, does NOT ease in. SOMETHING CHANGES EVERY THREE TENTHS OF A SECOND — that is at least THIRTEEN separate changes across the four seconds — and at every single instant AT LEAST THREE things are changing at once: the whole-body pose of the team, a present travelling downward, an elf travelling sideways, and a lighting effect somewhere else in the picture. There is no held frame, no pause, no settle: 0.0s — the clip opens mid-gallop: both reindeer already have their front legs tucked up and their hind legs kicked out, the sleigh already bobbing DOWN on the spot, TWO presents are already tumbling in mid-air below the sleigh and an elf is already sprinting in from the left with its arms out, AND the crescent moon is already flaring at double brightness with a ring of short spokes around it. 0.3s — the reindeer stretch out long, legs straight fore and aft, antlers levelled forward; the lower present lands in the left elf's arms and it bobs down hard with the weight; a fresh present tumbles out of the sack. 0.6s — the sleigh rocks hard to one side, Santa leaning right over with it and his beard swinging across; the left elf drops its present on the pile and waves both arms; a second elf sprints in from the right edge. 0.9s — Santa snaps the reins with both hands held LOW at his chest; a bright chase of colour runs along the whole team from the lead reindeer back to the sleigh; two presents tumble past each other in the air at different heights. 1.2s — both reindeer tuck their legs right up under them, bodies compressed, and the sleigh drops low on the spot; the right elf catches a present on the run without stopping; the moon strobes twice. 1.5s — Santa tips his head back and his belly bounces twice in a big laugh, hat bobble swinging low; two presents spill out of the sack together and tumble down side by side; the stars flash in alternating pairs. 1.8s — the reindeer kick their back legs out together, antlers dipping down and forward; both elves collide at the pile, bounce apart and scurry opposite ways; the whole team's outline flashes brighter one bulb row at a time. 2.1s — the sleigh tips nose-down and back level, Santa leaning forward over the reins with his sack rocking behind him; a present bounces once off the pile before settling; every star swaps colour gold to white. 2.4s — both reindeer switch to an opposite gallop phase, front and back legs crossing; a third elf runs in from the left; a chase of colour runs backwards from the sleigh to the lead reindeer. 2.7s — Santa throws both arms out LOW and wide at hip height, red jacket flashing brighter; three presents are in the air at once at three different heights; the moon drops to half and snaps back to full. 3.0s — the sleigh rocks hard the other way, runners swinging, the reindeer's heads swinging opposite; the elves jump on the spot together as a big present lands on the pile; the star trail strobes in sequence. 3.3s — the reindeer bunch up, legs folded tight; the growing pile of presents flashes in sequence left to right; two elves run out toward the edges while a fourth runs in. 3.6s — the reindeer stretch out at full gallop again, Santa's beard streaming back; a last pair of presents tumbles down and is caught; the stars twinkle out and back in a rolling wave the other way. 3.9s — the whole picture — Santa, the sleigh, both reindeer, every star, the crescent moon, the whole grown pile of presents and every elf still in frame — flashes together to maximum brightness twice in quick succession for the final beat. Every change is rendered by bulbs switching on and off row by row across the grid like an animated light-bulb sign — chunky and instantaneous, never smooth morphing, never a crossfade. The elves and the presents are drawn as chunky blocky bulb shapes with no facial detail. The coloured reflections on the driveway shift and ripple with every change. Notes from the round
What made it work

A crowd is safest from behind. About twenty neighbours, specified as rear and three-quarter-rear views in loose clusters with dogs, a phone filming and parked cars. Rear views were chosen deliberately to avoid twenty AI faces, and the crowd stays a silhouette bank that reads as a real bystander video.

Name the parts, not the object. “Make it clearly a Santa inflatable” does not work. Naming the fur trim, the belt buckle, the beard, the pom-pom and the wrinkled nylon is what makes it read as an inflatable Santa rather than a red shape.

g1 was passed a frame for SUBJECT AND ACTION ONLY. v23_c01_g1.png supplied the man, the faded inflatable and the ladder — with its camera explicitly excluded, because v27 needed a completely different wide angle from across the street.

What made it work

A falling object needs a side, a landing spot and a ban. Take 1 sent the inflatable up into the sky. The fix was to state which side it falls on (the same side as the man), where it lands, and that it must never travel upward — gravity is not implied by “falls”.

Hold the crowd facing away for the whole clip. “The neighbours in the foreground stay seen FROM BEHIND for the whole clip — no faces turn to camera.” A reaction beat is exactly where the model wants to turn them around. Reactions live in the audio instead: “Oh my God!”, “Whoa!”

THAT EXACT SIZE AND THAT EXACT POSITION ARE LOCKED from the first frame to the last. Nothing lit ever appears outside the curtain rectangle — not on the sage-green stucco, the gables, the roof, the sky, the spruce trees, the lamp post or the driveway. BECAUSE IT CANNOT GROW, ALL THE ENERGY GOES SIDEWAYS, DOWNWARDS AND INTO THE BULBS: twisting, leaning, squashing, dropping, spinning, skidding, flashing and chasing — never stretching upward. All their movement is in their bodies, not in their position. THE LIGHT PICTURE IS A LITTLE CARTOON THAT PLAYS OUT, NOT A PICTURE THAT SITS THERE FLASHING. This is a WIDE shot seen from the bottom of a driveway, so small pose flicker inside the artwork will not read at all. What reads at this distance is movement that TRAVELS across the picture. FOUR layers run at the same time for the whole four seconds, and all four are big, obvious movements: LAYER ONE — THE FIGHT ITSELF, in BIG whole-body redraws. Santa and the goblin trade slaps, shoves, headlocks and tugs on the sack, both leaning right over, both fully changing shape between beats: arms swung across, bodies bent double, one dropped into a crouch while the other rears back. Between one beat and the next the silhouette of each figure is unmistakably a different shape — never a small wobble. LAYER TWO — SANTA'S RED HAT FLIES BACK AND FORTH ACROSS THE TOP BAND. Knocked loose, it arcs from one side of the lit area to the other and back again across the four seconds, tumbling end over end as it goes, drawn by whole bulbs switching so it visibly somersaults rather than glides. It stays well below the top edge of the curtain at every moment and never leaves the rectangle. One of them swipes at it and misses each time it passes. LAYER THREE — PRESENTS BOUNCE OUT ALONG THE BOTTOM BAND. Chunky wrapped presents in bright red, green, gold and blue burst out of the sack one after another and BOUNCE sideways along the very bottom of the picture, hopping in visible arcs, a new one every half second, so at any instant two or three presents are in the air at different heights. They bounce only inside the rectangle and never fall out of the bottom of the curtain; they gather into a pile at the far corners that grows visibly wider across the four seconds, spreading SIDEWAYS only, never upward. LAYER FOUR — THE STAR-BURST PUMPS AND THE GOLD STARS STREAM. The white star-burst puff between them flashes and changes shape on every impact, and the scattered gold stars continuously chase around the pair, one lighting as the one before it goes out, an endless streaming ripple that never stops. the goblin plants both feet and hauls the other way, the sack stretching long between them, and every gold star twinkles out and back. 0.9s — the goblin lets go suddenly and Santa flies backwards onto his backside with both boots in the air, while the hat reverses direction and tumbles back the other way. 1.2s — Santa scrambles up on all fours and butts the goblin in the stomach; the goblin folds double with his eyes crossed, and the star-burst bursts to double size. 1.5s — they lock into a spinning tussle, arms tangled and both heads down, and the outline of both figures flashes brighter one bulb row at a time from the bottom upward. 1.8s — the goblin gets Santa in a headlock and rubs his knuckles on Santa's head; Santa's beard flies out sideways and his legs kick, and two more presents burst out and bounce along the bottom. 2.1s — Santa stamps on the goblin's bare green foot; the goblin shoots straight up rigid with his mouth wide open and both arms pinned to his sides, flashing green. 2.4s — the goblin hops on one foot clutching the other, and Santa snatches the sack back and hugs it to his chest, while a chase of colour runs UP the whole picture. 2.7s — the goblin dives at the sack and they both tip over sideways in a heap, boots and stubby green legs sticking out, and the gold stars strobe. 3.0s — they pop back up nose to nose, both leaning in hard with their fists up, and the star-burst flashes between them in alternating colours. 3.3s — Santa swings a huge roundhouse slap that spins the goblin right round on the spot twice, and the bouncing presents all flash colour at once. 3.6s — the goblin, still spinning, catches the flying hat on his own head and freezes mid-spin looking at it, while Santa points at him with both hands and the picture flashes in alternating vertical strands. 3.9s — Santa grabs his hat back and jams it on, both of them slumped and panting with the sack held between them, and the whole picture — Santa, the goblin, the sack, the presents, the star-burst and every gold star — flashes to maximum brightness twice in quick succession for the final beat. Every pose change is rendered by bulbs switching on and off row by row across the grid — chunky and instantaneous, never smooth morphing, never a crossfade, never a realistic animation curve. Coloured light spills and shifts across the driveway and over the backs of the crowd with every change. Other takes on disk (2)
v28_c01_g1.mp4job 5519c54f — The curtain was lifted straight up instead of dipping, and the crowd’s count was out of sync with the drop, so the 3-2-1 beat landed on nothing.
v28_c01_g2.mp4job 42ec09dd — “the boxes are too big” — then, once they were resized, “everything is good but it didn’t used our boxes.” The take invented its own packaging, which is why the packshot was attached to take 3.
Notes from the round
What made it work

Describe the whole reference back, then isolate the one change. The prompt is an explicit “EVERYTHING BELOW STAYS EXACTLY AS IN THE REFERENCE” inventory followed by a single “THE ONE CHANGE” block. Re-describing the reference in full is what stops the camera drifting while the model adds the new elements — first take, no re-roll.

What made it work

Constrain how many fit, not how big they are. “Smaller boxes” and stated dimensions both failed. What worked was giving the model a count against a landmark it can already see — how many boxes have to fit across the shelf — so the size falls out of the arithmetic instead of being guessed.

A reference cannot overrule what is already in the start frame unless you say so. The packshot was attached and still ignored, because the start frame already showed packaging and the model treated that as settled. The fix was to say out loud that the boxes in the start frame are replaced by the ones in @Image 2.

ABSOLUTELY NO ZOOM IN, NO ZOOM OUT, NO PUSH IN, NO PULL BACK, NO DOLLY, NO CRANE. The house and the garage door stay exactly the same size in frame from the first frame to the last. THE CROWD IS CASUAL, RELAXED AND ALREADY HAPPY — AND ALREADY MOVING IN THE VERY FIRST FRAME. This is not an audience waiting for something to happen. Nobody is standing frozen staring at the garage in anticipation, nobody holds still and then reacts, there is no build-up and no big synchronised cheer. They are neighbours hanging about on a driveway on a cold night, chatting to each other, laughing at each other, sipping drinks, glancing over at the lights and then back at their friends. Their attention drifts on and off the garage the whole time. They are ALL seen FROM BEHIND — no face is ever turned toward camera. AT 0.0s, IN THE VERY FIRST FRAME, EVERY PERSON IS ALREADY MID-MOVEMENT. There is NO still opening frame, NO frozen first beat, NO pause before the motion starts, NO moment where the group holds and waits. Someone is already mid-laugh, someone is already turning, someone is already raising a cup, a child is already bouncing. The clip starts in the middle of the action and never settles. CONTINUOUS OVERLAPPING MOTION, EVERY HALF SECOND, NEVER IN UNISON — at any instant several different people are doing several different things, and their little actions start and stop at different times so the group always looks alive: 0.0-0.5s — a child near the front is already bouncing on the spot and swings an arm up toward the garage mid-bounce; two adults beside them are mid-conversation, heads turned to each other, one shrugging. 0.5-1.0s — a woman in the centre laughs and rocks back on her heels, shoulders shaking; a man at the right is already filming on his phone and shifts his weight to his other foot; someone lifts a takeaway cup and drinks. 1.0-1.5s — the kids in the front row lean into each other and one points lazily at the lights without turning round; a teenager at the left shoves both hands deeper into their pockets, hunches, and blows out a long fog of breath. 1.5-2.0s — a woman at the left leans sideways into the person beside her and says something; they both laugh; another person scratches under their bobble hat and looks away from the garage entirely. 2.0-2.5s — two people knock shoulders and one claps once, casually; a child in a bobble hat twists round to tug a sleeve, then swings back; a couple sway slightly, arms linked. 2.5-3.0s — scattered easy laughter ripples through the group, a few loose claps at different moments, not together; one adult crouches down to say something to a kid; another points out at the lights with a cup still in hand. 3.0-3.5s — the man at the right lowers his phone, wipes his eyes laughing and says something sideways; a kid scrambles up onto their knees; two heads tip together. 3.5-4.0s — a few people applaud loosely, hats bobbing, breath fogging, someone waves an arm overhead at a neighbour, someone else is already turning to talk to the person behind them. Notes from the round
What made it work

A missing beat is a duration problem, not a wording problem. Three counted dips plus a reveal do not fit in 4s; g6 is the same shot at 5s and the third dip landed first try. Two takes were spent rewording before the duration was tried. Second lesson, from g10: a “change only X” prompt still needs the pose pinned by name — in g9 both hands were on the dome, in g10 only the right hand stayed on the knob.

THE MOTHER - a woman about 30 on the RIGHT, burgundy chunky cable-knit jumper, mid-blue straight-leg jeans, white low trainers. Their inner hands are clasped together above and behind the child. COUNT LOCK: exactly three people in the foreground. No fourth family member, no staff member walking into shot. [5] OBJECTS THE CUP - a tall clear plastic cold-cup of bright green iced matcha with a domed lid. It is a DRINK. It is not a match, not a matchstick, not a candle, not a stick of any kind. THE DISPLAY - a pyramid stack of our wide flat matte-black slab boxes standing upright on their long bottom edge with their printed front square to camera, on a low dark maroon riser, four tiers high, each box printed with a white condensed uppercase LED CURTAIN LIGHTS headline, a gold Create Your Own Magic subline and a red BEST SELLER corner ribbon. It stands at the far end of the aisle BEHIND the family, on the RIGHT side of that aisle, with a decorated Christmas tree beside it, exactly as in @Image 1. It is what THE CHILD looks back at. [6] LOCATION - a bright Christmas decorations shop: a glossy pale floor, decorated Christmas trees and dressed display tables down both sides, tall shelving on the LEFT only, warm shop lighting. All of it survives to the last frame. The top quarter of the frame stays clean and uncluttered. [7] FIRST FRAME - exactly the start image: the three of them mid-stride walking toward camera, the child between them holding THE CUP low in both hands, his head tipped up. [8] TIMELINE 0.0-0.4s - the camera is near-static at child height. All three keep walking toward camera in stride, THE CHILD holding THE CUP in both hands. 0.4-1.3s - ONE SINGLE FLOWING MOVEMENT WITH NO BREAK INSIDE IT, and no cut at any point in it. Still walking toward camera in stride, THE CHILD turns his head back over his LEFT shoulder, up the aisle behind him, straight at THE DISPLAY; his eyes go WIDE and his mouth falls open in amazement and delight; and WHILE HIS HEAD IS STILL TURNING his fingers are already loosening, so that the look and the loss of grip are one continuous action and not two separate events. THE CUP slips straight down out of both hands between his feet, lid first, turning once as it falls. He never looks at it - his eyes stay locked on THE DISPLAY from the moment he sees it. His feet keep walking right through all of it and the camera does not move. 1.3-1.8s - THE CUP hits the polished floor and bursts: a wide bright green splat spreads out across the pale floor, ice cubes skid away, the domed lid pops off and spins flat. THE CHILD's empty hands stay open at his sides and he keeps staring at THE DISPLAY, mouth open, oblivious to the mess. 1.6-2.2s - both adults stop dead mid-stride, their clasped hands pulling apart, and snap their heads DOWN to look at the child and the green splat. Their faces are SHOCKED - eyes wide, eyebrows up, mouths open; THE MOTHER's free hand comes up to her mouth, THE FATHER's shoulders drop. They stay where they are and keep staring down. 2.2-2.6s - while they are still staring, THE CHILD carries his head turn on into his body and turns his back to the camera in one continuous movement, already lifting his leading foot into the first step toward THE DISPLAY. 2.6-4.0s - THE CHILD walks away from camera up the aisle into depth, arms swinging, unbothered. The camera follows him from behind at his height with a natural handheld bounce, and drifts slightly RIGHT so THE DISPLAY comes into frame on the right. The parents fall away behind, still stopped. 4.0-5.0s - THE CHILD reaches THE DISPLAY, stops in front of it and throws BOTH arms straight up toward the third and fourth tiers of boxes, hands open, tipping his head back. He says his line here. The camera settles on him from behind with THE DISPLAY filling the right of frame, exactly the composition of @Image 1. The last frame holds on that. [9] CAMERA AND OPTICS - vertical 9:16, normal wide-angle phone lens at roughly child height. One continuous handheld take with a natural walking bounce. CAMERA LOCK: for the first 2.6 seconds the camera holds ONE position at child height - the framing of the start image - with nothing but a small handheld wobble. It does not step closer, does not back off, does not change height, does not swing, does not re-frame and does not change lens. Its only real move in the whole clip is the follow from behind after 2.6s, with a slight rightward drift onto THE DISPLAY. Normal wide-angle only - no fisheye, no barrel distortion, no curved shelving lines. No cut, no zoom, no orbit. [10] LIGHTING - bright even warm shop lighting, unchanged for the whole clip. [11] PHYSICS - THE CUP is a light plastic cup of cold liquid: it falls fast under real gravity, lands with a slap, and the drink bursts outward low and wide across the hard floor. The green splat is a shallow spill that stays on the floor; it does not fountain upward, does not splash onto the child or the adults, and does not reach their knees. The ice skids, it does not bounce high. Nothing flies up out of frame. [12] AUDIO - natural sound only: the flat hard slap of a plastic cup hitting a polished floor, the wet spread of liquid, ice skittering, quiet shop ambience and distant footsteps. At 4.2s THE CHILD says clearly in a small toddler voice: "Mama, I want it!" Nothing else is spoken. (no BGM). No subtitles. [13] POSITIVE LOCKS - real-time motion at normal speed throughout. Exactly three people. ONE CONTINUOUS TAKE WITH NO CUT ANYWHERE, AND THE SAME SHOP IN EVERY SINGLE FRAME. THE CUP is a green iced drink. THE CHILD SEES THE DISPLAY FIRST, IS AMAZED, AND ONLY THEN DROPS THE CUP - the look always comes before the drop, and the drop is an accident he never notices. The adults stop and stare down in shock. THE CHILD ends in front of the pyramid of matte-black boxes with both arms raised, seen from behind. The picture stays sharp to the last frame. DO NOT INCLUDE: any music, any song, any score, any soundtrack; a cut, an edit, a transition, a fade or a second shot; a cut between the look and the drop; any frame where the shop behind the family changes, swaps, re-arranges or becomes a different store; the camera jumping closer, changing height or re-framing during the first 2.6 seconds; slow motion; the child dropping the cup before he has looked back and seen THE DISPLAY; the child looking down at the cup, at his hands or at the floor at any point before 2.2s; the child throwing, tossing or deliberately releasing the cup; the child looking frightened, upset, guilty or about to cry instead of amazed; the adults walking on past without reacting; the adults kneeling down, picking the cup up, cleaning the floor or scolding him; the liquid splashing high, hitting the people, or reaching above knee height; the child crying; the child holding a match, a matchstick, a candle or a stick; a fourth person; the camera overtaking or getting in front of the child; on-screen text; subtitles.

What made it work

One continuous take needs the beats to overlap. Two adjacent beats that each describe a separate whole-body activity give seedance a seam to cut on; carrying the body motion straight across the boundary (“his head turn carries on into his body turn”) and banning cuts in HARD RULES removed it. Nothing flashes, strobes, blinks, twinkles or pulses. 0.00s — it lands out of the first frame already mid-move: the green character is already swinging forward through the bottom of his arc on the stretched white beard, both feet kicked out ahead of him, while Santa is already skidding a half-step to the right with both boots sliding on the ground line and both arms flung wider for balance. 0.25s — the green character swings forward on the stretched white beard, both green hands sliding a little further along it, both feet kicked out in front of him. 0.50s — Santa is hauled a step to the right, both boots skidding on the ground line, his arms flung wider for balance. 0.75s — the green character swings back the other way and both knees tuck right up to his chest. 1.00s — Santa plants both boots, leans right back against the pull and his mouth opens wider in a yell. 1.25s — the green character lets go with one hand, dangling from the other, and windmills his free arm. 1.50s — Santa's red hat tips down over one eye and he shoves it back up with one white glove. 1.75s — the green character grabs on with both hands again and bounces twice on the beard like a rope. 2.00s — the beard stretches visibly longer and Santa is dragged another step, one boot lifting off the ground line. 2.25s — the green character scissors both legs wide apart and snaps them back together, his grin stretching wider. 2.50s — Santa gets both white gloves onto his own beard and hauls back on it hand over hand. 2.75s — the green character is reeled in a whole body-length closer, still dangling, both huge white eyes going wide. 3.00s — he plants both pointed green shoes flat against Santa's chest and pushes off; the beard stretches taut again. 3.25s — Santa's arms fly straight up and he rocks back on his heels, both boots skidding backward. 3.50s — the green character swings out to full stretch on the end of the beard, body almost horizontal, his red hat tipping right back on his head. 3.75s — Santa bends his knees and hauls down hard with both fists; the green character drops and springs straight back up. 4.00s — everything peaks together: the beard stretched to its limit, the green character at full swing with both legs kicked out, Santa bent right back with both boots skidding and his mouth wide open — every limb still well inside the lit rectangle. Every pose change is rendered by bulbs switching on and off row by row across the grid like an animated light-bulb sign — chunky and instantaneous, never smooth morphing. The coloured reflections on the wet driveway shift and ripple with every change. DENSITY OF MOTION — HARD RULE: at every single moment of the four seconds, AT LEAST SIX DIFFERENT THINGS in the artwork are changing at once — Santa's arms, his boots, his red hat, his beard, his face, the green character's arms, his legs, his pointed shoes, his ears, his eyes, his grin and his red hat. The picture is never still for even one twentieth of a second. A calm, slow, sparse or barely-moving picture is a TOTAL FAILURE. This must read as frantic, laugh-out-loud cartoon slapstick with something big happening everywhere you look. CRITICAL — HOW THE LIGHTS MUST BE BUILT. BACKGROUND OVERRIDE, READ THIS FIRST: in this reference image the curtain carries a SOFT PASTEL BLUE, VIOLET AND PINK BACKGROUND FIELD filling the whole rectangle behind the two figures. That coloured background is part of the start image and it STAYS exactly as it is — it is the one and only exception to the line further down about solid saturated background fields. But it is still built out of individual countable bulbs on see-through vertical strands, never a smooth colour wash, never a flat painted panel and never a screen. Its colours may shift and ripple with the animation, but the field itself never becomes a solid glowing surface, and it never turns into a dirty grey haze or a muddy fog. Everything else in the block below applies exactly as written. The picture on the garage door is NOT an LED video wall, NOT a screen, NOT a projection. It is a hanging curtain of LED string lights: many thin vertical wires hung side by side from a header cable pinned under the garage lintel, each wire carrying small round bulbs. Build the whole picture out of VERTICAL DOTTED LINES OF LIGHT. The horizontal gap between neighbouring strands is visibly WIDER than the vertical gap between bulbs on the same strand, so the grid is tall and rectangular — never a square pixel matrix. The curtain is SEE-THROUGH. Through the gaps between strands you clearly read the garage door behind it: its horizontal panel seams, its trim, the faint shadows of the wires falling on it. Away from the coloured field the areas are NOT a solid painted surface — the unlit bulbs show as tiny dull grey dots and the thin dark wires as faint vertical lines. Every lit bulb is a tiny point source: blown-out white core, coloured halo bleeding around it, a small soft star flare, individually countable. The artwork is extremely low resolution and blocky — chunky stepped edges, no smooth curves, no thin outlines, no small facial detail, no gradients, no anti-aliasing. The curtain hangs a few inches proud of the door: the strands sag slightly, each strand ends at a slightly different height so the bottom hem is uneven and wavy, a faint breeze tilts the sheet, and the glow bounces back off the door behind it as a soft halo. Light spills onto the wet driveway in a speckled uneven pattern, not a flat even wash. ABSOLUTELY NO: LED video wall, TV screen, monitor, jumbotron, projector image, black backing panel, bezel or frame, dense square pixel grid, smooth clean vector artwork. Real amateur photo, natural noise, no CGI polish. ABSOLUTE HARD RULE — THE GARAGE DOOR IS THE ONLY LIT SURFACE. The artwork is hard-cropped at all four edges of the curtain. It NEVER grows, shrinks, shifts, warps or drifts. Nothing spills onto the slate-blue clapboard, the white trim, the projecting gable, the roof, the black pendant lantern, the bare winter tree or the sky. HARD RULES: nobody turns around, no face is shown toward camera. No new people walk into frame, and nobody leaves. No cars and no pets enter frame. NO TEXT, NO LETTERS, NO WORDS, NO NUMBERS, NO SIGNS anywhere in the light artwork, and no captions, subtitles or watermark anywhere in the video. AUDIO: natural room sound only — no music, no score, no background song. Cold outdoor night ambience, relaxed overlapping chatter, easy natural laughter, the odd loose clap, boots on wet tarmac, a faint electrical hum from the lights. LOOK: real iPhone UGC at night. Noisy shadows, blown highlights around the bulbs, natural handheld wobble, no cinematic grade, no lens flare, no slow motion, no speed ramp.

It is a hanging curtain of LED string lights: many thin vertical wires hung side by side from a header cable, each wire carrying small round bulbs. Build the whole picture out of VERTICAL DOTTED LINES OF LIGHT. The horizontal gap between neighbouring strands is visibly WIDER than the vertical gap between bulbs on the same strand, so the grid is tall and rectangular — never a square pixel matrix. The curtain is SEE-THROUGH. Through the gaps between strands you clearly read the garage door behind it: its seams, its trim, the faint shadows of the wires falling on it. The unlit areas are NOT a solid coloured field — they are simply dark wall, with the unlit bulbs showing as tiny dull grey dots and the thin dark wires as faint vertical lines. Every lit bulb is a tiny point source: blown-out white core, coloured halo bleeding around it, a small soft star flare, individually countable. The artwork is extremely low resolution and blocky — chunky stepped edges, no smooth curves, no thin outlines, no small facial detail, no gradients, no anti-aliasing. The curtain hangs a few inches proud of the wall: the strands sag slightly, each strand ends at a slightly different height so the bottom hem is uneven and wavy, a faint breeze tilts the sheet, and the glow bounces back off the wall behind it as a soft halo. Light spills onto the snow in a speckled uneven pattern, not a flat even wash. ABSOLUTELY NO: LED video wall, TV screen, monitor, jumbotron, projector image, black backing panel, bezel or frame, dense square pixel grid, solid saturated background field, smooth clean vector artwork. Real amateur photo, natural noise, no CGI polish. ABSOLUTE HARD RULE — THE ANIMATION STAYS INSIDE THE CURTAIN. THE BIGGER THE MOTION GETS, THE MORE STRICTLY THIS APPLIES. The lit rectangle is hard-cropped at all four edges like a bezel. It NEVER grows, shrinks, shifts, warps or drifts on the wall. No flung arm, no black boot, no green leg, no brown boot, no swinging red sack and no tumbling gold present ever touches or crosses outside the curtain rectangle. At every instant, in every pose, every figure keeps a clear margin of at least two full unlit strands of dark wall inside every edge of the curtain — top, bottom, left and right. If a swing, a windmill, a thrown-up arm or a bouncing present would reach an edge, THE POSE IS DRAWN SMALLER so it stays inside — the rectangle is never made bigger to fit it. Santa falls along the ground line and stays low; nothing is launched upward out of the picture. Nothing spills onto the grey shingle roof, the white window frames, the porch, the deep red front door, the sky or the evergreen. As the camera walks closer the bulb grid simply becomes coarser and the individual bulbs become bigger and more countable — the artwork does not gain detail and does not gain size. HARD RULES: no people, no cars, no pets enter the frame. NO TEXT, NO LETTERS, NO WORDS, NO NUMBERS, NO SIGNS anywhere in the light artwork, and no captions, subtitles or watermark anywhere in the video. AUDIO: natural room sound only — no music, no score, no background song. Cold quiet suburban night ambience, boots crunching rhythmically on packed snow with each stride, breath, a faint distant car, a faint electrical hum from the lights. No voice. LOOK: real iPhone UGC at night. Noisy shadows, blown highlights around the bulbs, slight motion blur on the walk, no cinematic grade, no lens flare, no slow motion, no speed ramp.
